How to Tell a Male Vs a Female Angelfish (all Differences)
Male vs. Female Molly Fish: How To Tell The Difference?
Lê Thế Lương * , Đinh Thế Nhân Diệp Nhựt Thái

facts.fact: Knowing the sex of livebearers early matters because male guppies can be sexually mature at about 3 months, so young fish may need separating.
Male guppies, mollies and platies have a gonopodium, an anal fin modified into a rod that can rotate to any angle and transfers sperm.
Female livebearers keep a triangular anal fin and are usually plumper than males.
Female guppies and some platies show a dark gravid spot low on the abdomen, which is the eyes of developing fry and indicates pregnancy.
Sexing young livebearers can take time and may need a magnifying glass.
Gestation after fertilisation: guppy 21-40 days, platy 30-40 days, molly 4-6 weeks.
A boxy, squared-off belly and a female hiding in plants or at the back of the tank signal that birth is near.
To avoid unwanted breeding, keep the sexes apart or buy only one sex; females store sperm and may keep producing broods for a while after separation.
Keep more than one female per male so no single female is harassed too much.
Sexing livebearers is harder than most people think; small or immature males whose anal fin has not yet become a gonopodium can be mistaken for females.
Practical Fishkeeping says livebearer 'sex change' has not been convincingly shown in the lab; reports may come from late-developing 'weak' male forms.

Some older female livebearers develop male-like colour, fins and behaviour through hormonal imbalance, but they cannot make sperm or form a working gonopodium, so they remain female (Practical Fishkeeping).
Platies (Xiphophorus) are too distantly related to hybridise with mollies or Endler's; guppy × molly hybrids are documented but rare.
Male mollies have a thin, elongated gonopodium; females lack it.
Female mollies grow larger, up to about 5 inches, while males reach about 3 inches.
Male mollies have larger, more elaborate dorsal fins that they show off during courtship; females' dorsal fins are smaller and simpler.
A ratio of one male molly to two or three females spreads out male attention and reduces stress.
Female bettas have a small pale 'egg spot' (ovipositor) between the ventral and anal fins; it is hard to see on white or pale fish.
Male betta fins can be three to four times longer than a female's, depending on type, and males have longer, thicker ventral fins.
Both betta sexes have a 'beard' (opercular membrane), but the male's is larger and may show even when not flaring; a female's shows only when she flares.
Female bettas are shorter and stockier; males are long and slender.
Female bettas ready to breed show dark vertical stripes on the body, which males do not.
Male bettas build bubble nests even without a female, though females sometimes build smaller ones.
Short-finned male bettas, such as koi bettas, can be hard to tell from females.
Juvenile bettas are nearly impossible to sex; wait two to three months.
Male and female bettas should not be kept together outside breeding; they fight and females often kill males.
Female betta sororities need at least five females; keeping just two females together is especially dangerous.
Wait until a betta is about two months old or mature before sexing it.
The female betta's white spot is hard to see on small fish; feeding the fish can make it easier to observe.
Betta colour changes with mood, so colour alone should not be used to sex the fish.
A mirror can trigger flaring to help sex a betta, but do not leave it for long because it stresses the fish.
A Vietnamese guide notes that shops mostly sell male bettas, while females are usually sold by hobbyists or higher-end shops; if unsure, assume a betta is male.
Mytour says adult female bettas are usually smaller than males.
A Vietnamese guide suggests using a magnifying glass (kính lúp) to check the anal fin of small guppies and mollies, and says platies and swordtails are sexed the same way.
Male angelfish often have a forehead bulge (nuchal hump) and a larger dorsal fin.
The angelfish breeding tube (genital papilla) sits on the underside, behind the ventral fins and in front of the anal fin.
The female angelfish's breeding tube is broad, cylindrical and blunt; the male's is thinner and pointed.
The angelfish breeding tube is most reliable during breeding; a female's may not show until she is full of eggs.
Angelfish physical sex differences usually appear at around six to seven months, later in some wild types; none work before maturity.
Males have a modest forehead bulge between the eyes and dorsal fin; females have a gentle backward-sloping forehead.
A swollen belly before spawning indicates a female angelfish full of eggs.
Angelfish sex differences are subtle and easy to misjudge even for experienced keepers; diet, environment, genetics and breed can mislead.
Chasing between angelfish that comes with conflict may mean two males, not a pair.
Angelfish tend to choose their own mates, so sexing alone does not guarantee a breeding pair.
A Can Tho University study on Pterophyllum scalare sexed fish after 90 days of age using external appearance and dissection of the gonads.
Female Corydoras grow longer than males (standard length); in some species by as much as 40%.
Seen from above, a female Corydoras is widest level with or slightly behind the ventral fin spines; a male is widest level with or just behind the pectoral fin spines.
Male Corydoras tend to have longer, pointed ventral fins; females' are fan-shaped and rounded; some species show no visible difference.
To sex Corydoras, feed them well for a while, then put them in a small container of tank water and look from above.
In some Corydoras species, males have black speckles on the pelvic fins while females' are clear.
